p: I must begin this essay with a confession of ignorance peculiar to my own date. In the year eighteen seventy-five, nobody in Europe knows that the great painted caves exist. Four years from now, in eighteen seventy-nine, a Spanish gentleman named Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola will take his little daughter Maria with him while he digs in a cave called Altamira, upon his estate in northern Spain. The child, wandering into a low side chamber with a lamp, will look up and cry out that there are oxen on the ceiling. There are: a whole herd of bison, painted in red and black, with the bulges of the rock used to give them form, so that they seem to swell and move in the flickering light.

Don Marcelino will publish his discovery, and the learned world of Europe will call him a fool or a forger. It was impossible, they said, that savages of the Stone Age could have painted with such skill. The paintings were too fresh, too fine, too modern. He will die in eighteen eighty-eight still disbelieved. Only in nineteen hundred and two, after similar paintings had been found in caves in France sealed under layers that no forger could have reached, did the most eminent of his critics, a Frenchman named Émile Cartailhac, publish an essay whose title, in French, means the confession of a sceptic. I record the story because it is a lesson to my profession. We are always too sure that people in the past were less capable than ourselves.

The pages from the future tell me of hundreds of decorated caves, most of them in France and Spain, though art of the same great age has since been found in many other parts of the world. The most celebrated is Lascaux, in the Dordogne region of south-western France, found in September of nineteen forty by four teenage boys, who, as the story is told, were following their dog, which had fallen into a hole. Its paintings are about seventeen thousand years old. There are horses, stags, bulls of enormous size, ibex, a bear, and, deep in a shaft, the only human figure of note: a man with a bird's head, apparently falling, before a wounded bison whose entrails hang out. Nobody knows what the scene means. Many have guessed.

Older still is the cave called Chauvet, also in France, discovered in nineteen ninety-four, where the paintings of lions, rhinoceroses, horses and bears are now thought to be more than thirty thousand years old. That is to say, the paintings at Chauvet are as far in time from the paintings at Lascaux as Lascaux is from ourselves. They are not crude beginnings. They are as accomplished as anything that came later.

The most surprising news in the Encyclopaedia concerns not Europe but the islands of the East Indies. In caves on the island of Sulawesi, painted scenes of animals, and of human or half-human figures apparently hunting them, have been dated by modern methods to more than forty thousand years ago, and on one account more than fifty thousand. In Spain, certain red markings have been claimed as the work of Neanderthals, older still, though this is disputed. The old picture of art beginning in France, which flattered the French and, it must be said, the rest of Europe, is no longer tenable.

The painters used pigments of the earth: red and yellow ochres, which are clays coloured by iron, black from charcoal or from a mineral called manganese, and occasionally white. They ground these, mixed them with water or perhaps animal fat, and applied them with fingers, pads of moss or fur, brushes of hair, and by blowing the paint through a hollow bone onto the rock, as one might blow through a straw. Among the most moving images in the whole of prehistory are the stencilled hands found in caves across the world, made by laying a hand against the rock and blowing paint around it. They are the signatures, if you like, of the artists; many of them, from the size of the hands, appear to be those of women and children.

They painted in darkness, by the light of lamps of stone in which animal fat burned upon a wick of moss or juniper. Some of the paintings lie far from the cave mouth, reached only by crawling through narrow passages. People did not live in these deep chambers. They visited them.

This is the question every visitor asks, and it has no settled answer. Early in the twentieth century, a French priest and scholar, the Abbé Henri Breuil, proposed that the paintings were hunting magic: that by depicting the animals, and sometimes depicting them wounded, the painters hoped to secure success in the chase. The difficulty is that the animals painted are not always the animals eaten; at Lascaux the bones in the cave are mostly of reindeer, but the paintings show few reindeer. Others proposed that the caves were sanctuaries, organised according to some scheme of male and female symbols. Others again have suggested that the painters were in a kind of trance, such as the priests or shamans of many hunting peoples enter, and that the strange dots and grids and half-human figures are the visions of that state. Each theory explains some of the evidence and none explains all of it.

I am content to remain uncertain. What strikes me is not the meaning but the fact. Some tens of thousands of years ago, human beings went down into the dark beneath the earth, with lamps of burning fat, and made images of the creatures they lived among, with such skill that a painter of the Royal Academy might envy them. They did it in many places, over an immense span of time, and for reasons that mattered so much to them that they risked the dark to do it. They were not savages. They were artists, and the world has not been without artists since.
